title: Events are the Wrong Abstraction for Your AI Agents - Mason Egger, Temporal.io

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that durable execution—not events—is the correct abstraction for building AI agents, with detailed coverage of crash-proof execution, automatic retries, state preservation, and the Temporal runtime. The content addresses a general infrastructure pattern for AI agent orchestration applicable across all verticals with no industry-specific focus. Prerequisites require basic understanding of distributed systems and event-driven architecture, placing this at an intermediate level. Recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer World's Fair with slides and live demo invitation. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct character-offset citations.

summary: Mason Egger opens with an analogy comparing geocentric and heliocentric models of the solar system, noting that both are accurate but the choice of frame of reference determines simplicity and utility. He applies this to AI agent architecture, asserting that scaling AI agents is the same distributed systems problem engineers have solved for decades. Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) has become the default pattern, but Egger challenges whether events should be at the center, noting that in typical EDA diagrams, more infrastructure handles events than implements core business logic. He identifies several problems: events sacrifice clear, well-defined APIs with no robust specification analogous to REST docs; business logic becomes scattered across services, making debugging require grep-ing through codebases; every service becomes an ad hoc state machine with local caches leading to race conditions and partial state updates; and most provocatively, EDA is tightly coupled at design time despite being loosely coupled at runtime—events function like global variables that can break unknown downstream consumers. Egger proposes reorienting around Durable Execution, which he describes as crash-proof execution enabling developers to focus on application goals rather than failure mitigation. He outlines four characteristics: automatic state preservation of all variables, function calls, inputs, and outputs; virtualized execution spanning multiple processes and machines that survives individual failures; resumption from the last known good save point, often without developer awareness; and time independence, enabling operations like sleeping for 30 days. Durable Execution is also hardware agnostic, building reliability into software rather than hardware. A durable execution agent architecture diagram is shown with a chat UI, durable workflow, and automatic retries for LLM and tool calls—much simpler than the EDA equivalent, letting developers focus solely on business logic. Egger reveals that durable execution still uses events under the hood but abstracts their complexity into the platform layer, comparing this to the historical progression of programming language abstractions from assembly to Fortran, Algol 60, Lisp, and object-oriented programming. Temporal provides this as an open-source, MIT-licensed product with seven SDKs (Go, Python, TypeScript, Ruby, .NET, Java, PHP) and natively polyglot function calls across languages. Egger closes by reiterating that all AI is distributed systems and invites attendees to try breaking his durable agent demo at the Temporal booth.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Geocentric vs. Heliocentric Analogy
sections.summary: Egger opens with a historical analogy: geocentric and heliocentric models are both accurate, but choosing the right frame of reference greatly simplifies understanding. He uses this to set up the argument that the software community may have the wrong abstraction at the center of AI agent architecture.

sections.title: AI Agents as Distributed Systems and EDA Definition
sections.summary: Egger connects the analogy to AI software, stating that scaling AI agents is no different from scaling microservices—it is the same distributed systems problem solved for decades. He shares Claude's definition of EDA as a pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events for loose coupling and asynchronous processing.

sections.title: EDA Architecture Example and Critique
sections.summary: An EDA-based AI agent architecture diagram is shown with cron jobs, a message bus, and a dead letter queue. Egger asks how much of this diagram is core business logic versus infrastructure to prevent breakage, arguing that events have become the center of the ecosystem instead of the actual logic being solved.

sections.title: Problems with Event-Driven Architecture
sections.summary: Egger enumerates EDA issues: sacrifice of clear APIs, scattered business logic across services requiring grep and runtime debugging, every service becoming an ad hoc state machine with local caches, lack of transactional consistency between messages and state updates, and race conditions leading to 2am pages.

sections.title: EDA Tightly Coupled at Design Time
sections.summary: Egger argues controversially that EDA is tightly coupled—loosely coupled at runtime but not at design time. He compares events to global variables: changing an event format can break unknown downstream consumers, making teams afraid to iterate on their architecture.

sections.title: Durable Execution Introduction and Characteristics
sections.summary: Egger introduces Durable Execution as crash-proof execution that lets developers focus on application goals rather than failure mitigation. He lists four characteristics: automatic state preservation of all variables and function I/O, virtualized execution across processes and machines, resume from last known good save point often without developer awareness, and time independence enabling operations like sleeping for 30 days. It is also hardware agnostic, building reliability into software rather than hardware.

sections.title: Durable Execution Agent Architecture
sections.summary: Egger shows a durable execution agent architecture diagram with a chat UI, durable workflow, automatic retries for LLM and tool calls, and audit storage. This diagram is much simpler than the EDA equivalent, letting developers focus solely on business logic without managing queues or events.

sections.title: Temporal Product and Polyglot Support
sections.summary: Egger introduces Temporal as an open-source, MIT-licensed product providing durable execution with seven SDKs (Go, Python, TypeScript, Ruby, .NET, Java, PHP) and another coming. He highlights natively polyglot execution—calling a Ruby function from Go code by providing function name and input parameters—and reveals that events still exist under the hood but their complexity is abstracted into the platform layer.

sections.title: Abstraction as Software Engineering Progress
sections.summary: Egger contextualizes durable execution within software engineering's 50-70 year history of abstracting complexity away from programmers: Fortran gave mathematical operations, Algol 60 and Pascal gave structured flow, Lisp gave garbage collection, Simula and Smalltalk gave OOP. Durable execution is the next abstraction, removing event and queue complexity from the developer's concerns.

sections.title: Closing
sections.summary: Egger reiterates that all AI is distributed systems under the hood and invites attendees to visit the Temporal booth to try breaking his durable agent demo, chat in the community Slack, or subscribe to the newsletter.
